newsitem.title: GERMANY: Southern Co. in group paying $1.9 billion for utility stake.
newsitem.headline: Southern Co. in group paying $1.9 billion for utility stake.

text.p: The city of Berlin said Tuesday it would sell a majority stake in its biggest utility, Bewag, to a group that includes Southern Co., the aggressive U.S. electric company, for about $1.9 billion.

Southern Co., one of the most active U.S. utilities in buying power-generating assets in other countries, agreed to buy the 50.8 percent stake in Bewag along with Germany's Veba AG and Viag AG for 2.9 billion marks ($1.7 billion), said Annette Fugmann-Heesing, a senior finance official in Berlin.
The three companies also will pay financially strapped Berlin another 290 million marks ($170 million) for other considerations.

Several Berlin senators had complained that Berliner Kraft und Licht AG, as Bewag is formally known, was worth more. The utility provides electricity and heat to more than 2 million households and thousands of companies in and around the city.

Berlin, whose dividing wall was a symbol of the Cold War until it came down in 1989, is struggling to plug a 5 billion mark ($2.95 billion) deficit and wants to sell nearly 6 billion marks ($3.5 billion) of assets this year.
Officials said the city was forced to sell the Bewag stake in a bid to avoid bankruptcy.

"Bewag is being sold primarily because the city is bankrupt or nearly bankrupt because the federal government has left us standing in the rain," Peter Strieder, a city official for the environment, told InfoRadio in Berlin.

Southern, based in Atlanta, will receive a 23.6 percent stake and management control of the company, Fugmann-Heesing said. Veba and Viag, which already each hold 10 percent stakes, will each receive an additional 13.6 percent, making their total stakes equal to Southern's.
Fugmann-Heesing said the three companies pledged to hold the stakes being sold for at least 20 years.
If the transaction is completed by year-end, the buyers will receive the 1997 dividend, she said. Berlin received a dividend payment of 45 million marks ($26.5 million) in 1996.

Berlin had hoped several German and foreign utilities would compete in an aggressive round of bidding for Bewag. But many potential foreign bidders dropped out when it emerged that Veba and Viag had acquired rights of first refusal more than 50 years ago.
Rather than bid against each other, Veba, Viag and Southern made a joint bid for Bewag. Power marketer Enron Corp. of Houston pulled out of the bidding in January.
Spurred by deregulation and slow growth in home markets, American utilities have been looking for mergers at home and abroad.

Southern has been one of the most active. It bought an 80 percent stake in Consolidated Electric Power Asia Ltd., an Asian power producer, in January for $2.7 billion and in 1995 paid $1.8 billion for Britain's South Western Electricity.

The sale of the Bewag stake is subject to approval by regulators. European Union authorities were expected to approve the deal, Fugmann-Heesing said. But if the case is referred to German authorities, it may run into trouble.
The German antitrust agency has already expressed doubts about the sale.

"The European cartel authorities will examine the sale first," Fugmann-Heesing said. "I expect a positive decision. But if there is a decision to pass the sale to the German cartel agency, then I expect it to be rejected."

Bewag had sales of 4.3 billion marks ($2.5 billion) last year and net profit of 170 million marks ($100 million). Electricity in Berlin costs 22.7 pfennigs (13.4 cents) per kilowatt hour -- the highest in Germany.

Already over 50 billion marks ($29.5 billion) in debt, Berlin has been forced to make big cuts in spending that have caused tensions to flare between the formerly communist eastern half of the city and the western half of Berlin, long pampered by generous subsidies from Bonn during the Cold War.
Southern Co.'s stock lost 25 cents to trade at $21 on the New York Stock Exchange.
